title: Gradient Descent: a Tour with Interactive Plots
text:
Gradient descent is arguably one of the most fundamental bricks of modern ML — linear regression, deep nets, and trillion-parameter LLMs all stand on top of it. In this post I won’t dig into the math behind the algorithm (I assume you’ve got that already) — just a quick reminder of the intuition before we jump to the most fun part: a 3D loss surface with local minima, where you can see exactly why plain GD struggles on non-convex problems.
The intuition: picture a hiker caught by a thunderstorm in the mountains. Pitch dark, pouring rain, thunder rolling — they need cover fast, and the only sensible strategy is to head somewhere lower where there’s at least some shelter from the wind. No map, the flashlight is soaked and dead — but they can feel the slope of the ground underfoot. They take a step in the downhill direction (step length = \(\alpha\), the learning rate), feel the slope again, step again. They keep going until everything around feels “uphill” — they’ve reached a basin. If it’s the only basin on the ridge — that’s the global minimum, hooray. If there are several (and in real terrain there usually are, as in the examples below) — they’ll end up in the closest one. Whether that’s good or bad depends on the circumstances.

title: Gradient Descent: a Tour with Interactive Plots
text:
Non-convex landscape: a 3D demo
Linear regression’s MSE is convex with a single global minimum. Real landscapes are messier — for instance,
\[
F(x, y) = \sin(\tfrac{1}{2}x^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}y^2 - 1)
       \cdot \cos(2x + 1 - e^y) \cdot x
\]
has a handful of local minima and saddle points. Real-world ML landscapes are typically much worse, with local minima, saddle points and flat plateaus where plain GD struggles. To get a feel for it, below is a set of classic optimization benchmarks. Pick a function from the dropdown, choose a starting point / step size / number of iterations, and hit Start. The surface is interactive (drag to rotate, scroll to zoom); the slider and ▶ button replay the descent step-by-step.

What’s in the menu
Sin-cos product — our starting example: \[F(x,y) = \sin\!\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}x^2 - \tfrac{1}{4}y^2 - 1\bigr)
       \cdot \cos(2x + 1 - e^y) \cdot x\] A handful of local minima and saddle points on \([-4, 4]^2\).
Himmelblau: \[F(x,y) = (x^2 + y - 11)^2 + (x + y^2 - 7)^2\] Four identical global minima at the corners. Which well GD falls into is entirely determined by the starting point.
Rastrigin — the classic “egg-crate”: \[F(x,y) = 20 + x^2 + y^2 - 10\bigl[\cos(2\pi x) + \cos(2\pi y)\bigr]\] Dozens of local minima on a grid; global minimum at the origin. Without momentum/adaptive methods, GD settles into the first hole it sees.
Ackley: \[F(x,y) = -20\, e^{-0.2\sqrt{(x^2+y^2)/2}}
         - e^{[\cos(2\pi x) + \cos(2\pi y)]/2} + e + 20\] Global minimum at the origin, surrounded by ripples of small wells. A favorite test for adaptive optimizers.
Six-hump camel: \[F(x,y) = \bigl(4 - 2.1x^2 + \tfrac{x^4}{3}\bigr)x^2 + xy + (-4 + 4y^2)y^2\] Six local, two global minima. Purely polynomial — the basin transitions are very visible.
Beale: \[F(x,y) = (1.5 - x + xy)^2 + (2.25 - x + xy^2)^2 + (2.625 - x + xy^3)^2\] A “banana valley” — long narrow canyon along which plain GD crawls in zig-zags. Classic scenario where momentum/Adam fly far faster.
Schaffer N2: \[F(x,y) = 0.5 + \frac{\sin^2(x^2 - y^2) - 0.5}{[1 + 0.001(x^2 + y^2)]^2}\] Global min at \((0,0)\). Concentric high-frequency oscillations near the origin — GD easily lands in one of the ring-shaped local minima.
Eggholder: \[F(x,y) = -(y+47)\sin\!\sqrt{|y+x/2+47|} - x\sin\!\sqrt{|x-(y+47)|}\] A chaotic landscape with many local minima; the global one sits on the boundary at \((512, 404.23)\). One of the toughest benchmarks out there.
Levi N13: \[F(x,y) = \sin^2(3\pi x) + (x-1)^2[1 + \sin^2(3\pi y)] + (y-1)^2[1 + \sin^2(2\pi y)]\] Global min at \((1, 1)\). Regular grid of local minima under an overall parabolic envelope.
Bukin N6: \[F(x,y) = 100\sqrt{|y - 0.01x^2|} + 0.01\,|x + 10|\] Global min at \((-10, 1)\). A very narrow ridge along the parabola \(y = 0.01x^2\) — classic test for valley-following descent.
Rosenbrock — the “banana function”: \[F(x,y) = (1-x)^2 + 100(y - x^2)^2\] Global min at \((1, 1)\). Parabolic valley whose floor is \(y = x^2\) — the most famous optimizer benchmark from the 1960s.
Booth: \[F(x,y) = (x + 2y - 7)^2 + (2x + y - 5)^2\] Global min at \((1, 3)\). A plain convex quadratic — useful sanity check: GD should find it within a handful of steps.

The surface below is interactive — drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. Markers: 🟢 start, 🔶 finish of the trajectory.



Show code (Python: default surface)
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
from IPython.display import HTML, display

pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"


def F_sincos(x, y):
    return np.sin(0.5 * x**2 - 0.25 * y**2 - 1) * np.cos(2 * x + 1 - np.exp(y)) * x

def grad_sincos(x, y):
    """Analytical gradient of Sin-cos product (for the initial trajectory)."""
    u = 0.5 * x**2 - 0.25 * y**2 - 1
    v = 2 * x + 1 - np.exp(y)
    su, cu = np.sin(u), np.cos(u)
    sv, cv = np.sin(v), np.cos(v)
    return (
        x**2 * cu * cv - 2 * x * su * sv + su * cv,
        -0.5 * x * y * cu * cv + x * np.exp(y) * su * sv,
    )


def make_trajectory(F, grad_F, x0, y0, alpha=0.1, n_steps=120):
    xs, ys, zs = [x0], [y0], [F(x0, y0) + 0.1]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        gx, gy = grad_F(xs[-1], ys[-1])
        xs.append(xs[-1] - alpha * gx)
        ys.append(ys[-1] - alpha * gy)
        zs.append(F(xs[-1], ys[-1]) + 0.1)
    return xs, ys, zs


COLORSCALE = [
    [0.00, "#000003"],   # near-black
    [0.12, "#1a0030"],   # very dark purple
    [0.25, "#3e0e7a"],   # purple
    [0.38, "#3b3a98"],   # indigo
    [0.52, "#2563eb"],   # blue
    [0.65, "#0ea5e9"],   # cyan-blue
    [0.76, "#22c55e"],   # green
    [0.85, "#facc15"],   # yellow
    [0.93, "#f97316"],   # orange
    [1.00, "#dc2626"],   # red
]

x_grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 120)
y_grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 120)
Xg, Yg = np.meshgrid(x_grid, y_grid)
Zg = F_sincos(Xg, Yg)

xs, ys, zs = make_trajectory(F_sincos, grad_sincos, x0=2.54, y0=-1.25,
                             alpha=0.1, n_steps=120)

fig = go.Figure([
    # 0 — surface
    go.Surface(x=Xg, y=Yg, z=Zg, colorscale=COLORSCALE, opacity=0.92,
               showscale=False, name="F(x, y)"),
    # 1 — trajectory line (hidden from legend)
    go.Scatter3d(x=xs, y=ys, z=zs, mode="lines+markers",
                 line=dict(color="#ef4444", width=4),
                 marker=dict(size=3, color="#ef4444"),
                 name="Trajectory", showlegend=False),
    # 2 — start (green circle)
    go.Scatter3d(x=[xs[0]], y=[ys[0]], z=[zs[0]], mode="markers",
                 marker=dict(size=8, color="#22c55e", symbol="circle",
                             line=dict(width=2, color="white")),
                 name="Start"),
    # 3 — finish (gold diamond)
    go.Scatter3d(x=[xs[-1]], y=[ys[-1]], z=[zs[-1]], mode="markers",
                 marker=dict(size=10, color="#fbbf24", symbol="diamond",
                             line=dict(width=2, color="white")),
                 name="Finish"),
])
fig.update_layout(
    title="F(x, y) surface and a gradient-descent trajectory",
    height=620, margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0),
    scene=dict(xaxis_title="x", yaxis_title="y", zaxis_title="F",
               camera=dict(eye=dict(x=1.6, y=1.6, z=0.9))),
)

The algorithm got stuck in a local minimum — a typical picture in non-convex problems (think neural networks), along with plenty of other unpleasant scenarios: extremely slow convergence, bouncing “wall to wall”, and so on — you likely saw some of them firsthand if you played with the functions above. To fight these headaches people came up with stochasticity, momentum, restarts, and a long list of heuristics that keep modern deep learning afloat.
